evidence: The rejected response rebases history instead of inspecting commits absent from main.
The rejected --user flag restricts results to the per-user manager instead of all system units requested.
The rejected glob lacks zsh's N qualifier, so no matches cause expansion failure rather than a harmless no-op.
The rejected response sorts by percentage rather than resident bytes and requests ten lines including the header, yielding only nine processes.
The rejected revision ordering does not transplant feature commits after old-base onto main.
The rejected glob omits the regular-file qualifier and can include executable directories.
The rejected response does not use brew uses --installed and therefore does not answer which installed formulae depend on the target.
The rejected plain numeric sort orders whole ps lines by their leading PID rather than sorting the RSS field.
BSD sed requires the explicit empty backup suffix after -i; the rejected form consumes the program as that suffix.
The rejected findmnt invocation omits both the OPTIONS column argument and the mount target.
The rejected fixed record-number test does not print an inclusive marker-delimited range or re-arm for later ranges.
The rejected *.txt pattern filters by suffix and does not enforce that every result is a regular file.
The rejected response repeats -o so operands are consumed as output paths and does not form a valid traced program invocation.
The rejected paste invocation invents unsupported flags and omits the input file whose lines must be joined.
The rejected -d option discards punctuation from comparison, changing ordering beyond the requested case folding.
The rejected response pipes device information into dd and writes an image when the task only asks to inspect devices.
The rejected -k option has no keyword expression and cannot select matching test names.
The rejected response omits -m, so go mod why interprets its operand as a package rather than answering why a module is required.
The rejected substitution replaces unrelated text instead of appending a line after each matching marker.
The rejected -p option lacks its required priority operand, making the command invalid.
The rejected response does not pipe the line-buffered program anywhere, so it does not demonstrate or satisfy the requested piped-output workflow.
The rejected short -b options all bind as body text, leaving the base branch and title requirements unsatisfied.
The rejected response neither sorts directory sizes nor limits output to the largest consumers.
The rejected -a requests system-wide collection and lacks the -- workload boundary before ./app.
The rejected awk program prints every record and never excludes the CSV header.
The rejected command selects only column two instead of using --complement to drop it.
The rejected tr invocation is malformed and omits the lowercase, numeric sorting, and top-twenty pipeline stages.
The rejected response omits the api.service unit filter and uses non-journal field names instead of the requested canonical fields.
The rejected command searches log files and never uses zsh's newline-splitting parameter-expansion flag to build the requested array.
The rejected response does not explicitly exclude version-control metadata and provides no evidence its separate exclude file does so.
The rejected awk and sort stages do not correctly aggregate byte totals per client or select the twenty largest totals.
The rejected diff has only one process-substitution operand and therefore cannot compare two sorted directory listings.
